en: Having prostrated before the one, the manifold, the true deity, the Supreme Brahman,
Āryabhaṭa declares these three: calculation, the measurement of time, and the celestial sphere.
In a *varga*, the letters of that *varga* [are used]; in an *avarga*, the letters of the *avarga*; from *ka* [onward], *ṅmau* and *yas*.
In the second and ninth squares, there are nine vowels; in an *avarga*, nine [consonants]; or in the final *varga*, nine [vowels].
In the past, the number of revolutions of the planets in a yuga were as follows: for the Sun, *khyughṛ*; for the Moon, *śaśi cayagiyiṅuśuchlṛ*; for Mars, *ṅiśibuṇḷṣkhṛ*; for Saturn, *ḍhuṅvighva*;
for Jupiter, *khricyubha*; for Mars [repeated], *bhadlijhnukhṛ*; and for Venus, Mercury, and Rāhu, [the same].
The moon’s apogee moves eastward at 0° 2' per day; Mercury at 0° 18' 30"; Venus at 0° 37' 30"; and the remaining planets, including the Sun, at 0° 59' 20".
The nodes move westward at these same rates, starting from the rising of Aries and the Sun in Laṅkā on the day of Mercury.
The Manus, the Manvantaras, and the elapsed portions of those Manvantaras;
the Yuga-feet at the beginning of the Kalpa, and [the duration] from the day of Brahmā until before the *Bhārata* war.
The moon’s zodiacal signs are twelve, its circle consists of degrees, minutes, and seconds, and these are multiplied by twenty-four.

By means of the breath (*prāṇa*), it traverses a minute (*kalā*) and a sign (*bhā*) in forty-eight degrees; the speed of the planets is [calculated] in sixty degrees of a sign, and the sun [traverses] one degree in sixty breaths.
The circumference of the earth is 3,200 *yojanas*. The distance between the sun and the moon is 4,800 *yojanas*. Mount Meru is 84,000 *yojanas* [high].

The planets—Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, Saturn, and Mars—are situated at intervals of 13, 22, 32, 46, and 57 degrees respectively, measured from the sun. Their conjunctions with the sun are equal [in duration] to their respective degrees.
The degrees of the planets' apogees are 9, 6, 10, 12, 9, and 3; the lunar latitude from the ecliptic is 4°30';
and the dimensions in *hasta*s are 12, 11, 10, 9, 12, and 14 for Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon, respectively.
Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, having reached the ninth, tenth, seventh, sixth, and eighth degrees [respectively] from the Sun, are the first nodes;
likewise, their apogees are at twelve, twenty-two, thirty, forty-two, fifty-four, and ninety degrees.
The half-measures of Jupiter (Jha) constitute the *Mandavṛtta* from the Moon; [the sequence] Śa, Ga, Cha, Gha, Ḍha, and Cha follows as previously stated.
Likewise, Jhā, Gḍa, Glā, Rḍha, and Dḍa follow from Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, the exaltations, and the swiftest planets respectively.
In the second and fourth quarters, the letters ṅa, kha, da, ja, and ḍa belong to the slow-moving [planets] when they are retrograde;
jā, ṇa, kla, chla, and jhna belong to the fast-moving [planets] from the ascending node; and gi, yiṅ, iśa, ku, vāyu, kakṣyā, and antya belong to the [other] fast-moving [planets].
*makhi*, *bhaki*, *phakhi*, *dhakhi*, *ṇakhi*, *ñakhi*, *ṅakhi*, *hasjha*, *skaki*, *kiṣga*, *śghaki*, *kighva*,
*ghlaki*, *kigra*, *hakya*, *dhaki*, *kica*, *sga*, *jhaśa*, *ṅva*, *kla*, *pta*, *pha*, *cha*— these are the sines of half-arcual measures (*kalā*).

Having understood this *Daśagītikā-sūtra*— the movement of the earth and the planets within the cage of the asterisms (*bha-pañjara*)— one who knows the revolution of the hosts of planets and asterisms goes forth, having pierced through to the Supreme Brahman.
Having paid homage to Brahmā, Kuja, Śaśin, Budha, Bhṛgu, Ravi, Kuja, Guru, Koṇa, and Bha, Āryabhaṭa here proclaims the knowledge honored in Kusumapura, according to the Gaṇitapāda.
One, ten, a hundred, a thousand, an ayuta, a niyuta, and likewise a prayuta;
a koṭi, an arbuda, and a vṛnda—each successive place is ten times the preceding one.
A square is a figure with four equal sides, and its area is the product of two equal quantities.
The product of three equal quantities is a cube; likewise, it would have twelve sides.
One should always take the square root by means of a double square root from the non-square portion;
when a square is subtracted from a square, the quotient is the square root in the next position.
One should subtract from the second cube the square of the cube root multiplied by three;
the square [of the remainder] multiplied by three times the previous [root] is to be subtracted from the first [square], and the cube [of that result] from the cube.
The body of the result for a triangle is the product of half the base and half the height;
its cube is half the product of the height and that [body], and it is a hexagon.
The area of a circle is the product of half its circumference and half its diameter;
the volume of a sphere is that same area multiplied by its own square root, without remainder.
When the side [length] is multiplied by the length and divided by their product, it is the diagonal line;
when the width is multiplied by half the length, the result should be known as the area of the field with respect to the length.
Having established the result for all fields on the side, that [result] is the square of the side;
the sine of one-sixth of the circumference is equal to half the diameter.
The circumference of the circle is approximately one hundred and sixty-two thousand, eight hundred and four yojanas, for that whose diameter is twenty thousand [yojanas].
One should cut off a quarter of the circumference of a circle from both a triangle and a quadrilateral;
however, the half-chords of equal arcs may be taken as desired within half the diameter.
From the first half-chord of the bow, by those [factors] by which the second half is diminished and cut away,
the remaining [halves] are each lessened by those respective portions of the first half-chord.
The circumference is to be determined by means of a circle, and the four sides by means of the two diagonals;
the level ground is to be determined by water, and the verticality by means of a plumb line.
Having added the square of the shadow to the square of the gnomon’s measure,
the square root of that result is half the diameter of its own circle.
The product of the gnomon and the sine [of the altitude] divided by the difference between the gnomon and the base—
whatever is obtained therefrom should be known as the shadow of the gnomon measured from its own base.

The difference between the tips of the shadows multiplied by the shadow, divided by the [other] shadow, is the *koṭi*. That *koṭi* multiplied by the gnomon and divided by the shadow becomes the *bhuja*.
The square of the base (bhuja) and the square of the perpendicular (koṭi) together constitute the square of the hypotenuse (karṇa).
In a circle, the product of the arrow (śara) and the diameter is indeed equal to the square of the half-chord (ardhajyā) of the arc.
When two revolutions are less than a *grāsa*, one should divide them separately by the multiplier of the *grāsa*.
The results obtained from the sum [of the revolutions] minus the *grāsa* are the *saṃpāta* and the *śara* respectively.
The desired [number] minus one, halved, increased by the preceding [number], and multiplied by the subsequent factor, with the face added, is the middle [term].
Alternatively, the desired number multiplied by the desired [number], or else the product of the beginning and end divided by half the number of terms, is the desired wealth.
From the square of the number increased by eight times its own value, added to the squares of the successive differences starting from double that value, take the square root;
subtract the initial double value and divide by one's own subsequent value; this result, increased by half a unit, is the desired term.
When the series beginning with one and increasing by one (1, 2, 3, ... is multiplied successively by three, the result divided by six is the "sum of squares" (*citighana*);
this is equal to the cube of the sum of the terms minus one, or it is the cube root of that sum minus one.
The sixth part of the triple product of the sequence of one, the same, and the step, shall be the square of the pile,
the cube of the pile, and the cube of the pile of the pile.
For one should subtract the product of the groups from the group of the products;
whatever remains as half of that, one should know to be the product of the multipliers.
From the product of two squares increased by the square of their difference, take the square root;
that [root], added to or subtracted from the difference and halved, yields the two factors.

The square root of the product of the constant term and the coefficient of the square, increased by half the square root of the constant term, is then diminished by its own square root and divided by the coefficient;
this result is the square root of the original constant term.
Then, having multiplied that result-quantity of the three-term proportion by the required quantity,
the quotient obtained when divided by the measure shall be this required result.
The denominators of the multipliers and divisors become mutually multiplied by each other's denominators;
that state of having a common denominator occurs when they are mutually multiplied by their respective denominators.
Multipliers become divisors, and divisors become multipliers;
that which is an addition becomes a subtraction, and a subtraction becomes an addition when reversed.
The accumulated wealth from each journey, diminished by the respective heap [of expenses], when divided individually by one less than the number of stages,
thus constitutes the total wealth.
One should divide the difference in value between two persons by means of the *gulikā*;
if the resulting price of the *gulikā* is equal to the actual value [of the object], it is correct.
When the quotient of the division is retrograde, the two times of conjunction—
past and future— are obtained by adding and subtracting the difference of motion from the time of conjunction in direct motion.
One should divide the portion of the greater numerator by the portion of the lesser numerator;
the remainder, multiplied by the denominator and added to the difference between the numerators, is [the result].

The product of the lower and upper [quantities], divided by the divisor obtained from subtracting the final addend, is the remainder; this remainder multiplied by the divisor of the greater addend, with the divisor of the two added to the greater addend, [is the result].

Regarding the section on the determination of time (kāla-kriyā-pāda): A year consists of twelve months; a month consists of thirty days. Sixty nāḍīs constitute a day, and sixty vināḍikās constitute a nāḍī.
Sixty long syllables constitute one *vināḍikā* of the asterisms, or else six breaths (*prāṇas*).
Thus is the division of time; likewise, the division of space [is determined] from the circle of asterisms (*bha-gaṇa*).
Those groups of *bha*-gaṇas which remain as differences between every two pairs [of revolutions] are the *yuga*-conjunctions;
and the groups of solar and lunar asterisms, when combined, are the *vyatīpātas*.
The signs of one’s own exaltation multiplied by their respective signs, then distinguished by their own signs, and multiplied by the revolutions of their own exaltations and debilitations;
the signs of Jupiter multiplied by the signs [of the zodiac], beginning with Aśvinī, constitute the years of Jupiter.
The revolutions of the sun are the solar years; the sum of the sun and moon [revolutions] are the lunar months;
the sum of the sun and earth [revolutions] are the days; and the revolutions of the asterisms are the sidereal days.
In a yuga, those intercalary months which are in excess of the solar months are to be known as lunar days;
these are diminished by the terrestrial days, resulting in the destruction of the lunar dates (tithis).
A solar year is human; that same [year] multiplied by thirty becomes a paternal (pitrya) year.
A paternal year multiplied by twelve is declared to be a divine (divya) year.
A divine thousand years constitutes a *yuga* common to the planets;
multiplied by twelve, it is one thousand and eight *yugas* of the planets, which forms a single day of Brahmā.
The first half of the *yuga* is an *utsarpiṇī* (ascending), and the latter half is an *apasarpiṇī* (descending).
Within the *yuga*, there is a period of perfect happiness (*suṣamā*) in the middle; at the beginning and the end, there is misery (*duṣṣamā*), due to the rising of the moon.
When sixty-six years and three quarters of a yuga had passed,
then twenty-three years of my life had elapsed here on earth.
The yugas, years, months, and days began simultaneously with the start of the bright fortnight of Caitra;
this time, which is without beginning or end, is inferred by the planets within their field.
The planets, revolving in their own orbits at a speed equal to that of the celestial sphere, complete the circumference of the earth in sixty solar years,
and they likewise traverse the circumference of the sky.
The Moon fills its small orb below in a short time;
however, the slow-moving [Saturn], being above all the others, fills its large orb in a long time.
For in a small mandala, the zodiacal signs (rāśis) are small, and in a large one, they are large;
likewise, the degrees (aṃśas) and minutes (kalās) are to be understood as being proportionally equal within their respective spheres.
Below the spheres [of the planets] are Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon;
and below these is the Earth, acting as their axle, situated in the center of space.

These seven, beginning with Saturn, are the lords of the hours (horās) in their respective order as swift-moving planets; from sunrise, the fourth planets in this sequence of swift motion become the lords of the day (dinapās).
All the planets revolve in their own orbits within the circle of the girdle;
they move in direct order from the apogee of slow motion (manda-ucca) and in retrograde order from the apogee of swift motion (śīghra-ucca).
Each of their respective epicycles is equal to its own circle of latitude;
the center of each epicycle is displaced from the center of the solid earth.
The semi-diameter of the circle of apsis is equal to half the difference between the [mean] orbit and the [mean] earth-distance;
the planets move along the circumference of that circle according to their mean motion.
That planet which has a swift motion when at its own apogee, a retrograde motion on its circular orbit,
and a slow motion when moving in direct motion on that same circle, is [the one under consideration].
The direct motions proceed from the slow [apex] and the retrograde motions from the fast [apex];
the mean position of a planet is at the center of its own orbit where it touches the circle of the epicycle.
From the slow-movement apogee (mandocca), there shall be loss of wealth and the loss of that wealth; from the fast-movement apogee (śighrocca), it is the reverse.
For Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, half of the [calculated] amount is deducted from the slow apogee as debt, while the former [amount] becomes wealth.
From the apogee of the slow motion and from the apogee of the fast motion, there is respectively a debt and a credit of half [a sign] for the planets that move slowly;
from the apogee of the slow motion the mean positions are known as the true positions, and from the apogee of the fast motion the [true] positions are to be understood.
From the swifter apogee, half [the equation] less should be subtracted as a debt; from its own slower apogee, it should be added as a credit.
However, for Venus and Mercury, the true [mean] positions are derived from the established slow apogees.
The difference between the true star and the planet, multiplied by its own epicycle and divided by half the circumference of the sky, becomes the velocity of the planet in its orbit;
this is the slow [motion] at the apogee and perigee.
From Aries to Virgo, the half of the northern colure extending from the equator is equal;
from Libra to Pisces, the remaining half extends southward.
The stars, the planets, the moon, and the node revolve incessantly in the apamaṇḍala (the ecliptic), as does the sun;
and within that half-circle from the sun, the shadow of the earth revolves.
Due to the node (pāta) of the apamaṇḍala, the moon moves to the north or south;
so too do Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, as well as Mercury and Venus due to their swift apogee (śīghrocca).
The Moon, when not separated by twelve degrees and situated at an interval from the Sun, is visible;
Venus is visible when separated by nine degrees; and the others [the planets] are visible when separated by increments of two degrees more than those [preceding them], respectively.
The hemispheres of the earth, the planets, and the stars are deprived of their color by their own shadows; the other hemispheres, facing the sun, shine according to their respective substance.
In the center of the cage of the zodiacal signs, situated in the middle of the sky and encircled by its latitudinal bands,
the terrestrial globe— composed of earth, water, fire, and air— is spherical on all sides.
Just as the bud of a kadamba flower is covered on all sides with blossoms,
so indeed is the terrestrial globe covered by all beings, both aquatic and terrestrial.
Above the earth, there is an increase of one *yojana* per day of Brahmā;
there is a decrease of one *yojana* per night equal to a day, as it is worn away by soft soil.
Just as one standing on a boat perceives the fixed stars as moving in the opposite direction,
so too do the fixed stars appear to move westward at an equal rate from Laṅkā.
Driven by the wind in a constant flow as the cause of its rising and setting, the stellar sphere,
together with the planets, revolves moving westward at the same speed as Laṅkā.
Mount Meru, one *yojana* in measure, is radiant and surrounded by the Himavat;
it is composed of jewels and is perfectly circular in every direction in the midst of the Nandana grove.
Mount Meru stands in the midst of the dry land, and the submarine fire (Baḍavāmukha) is in the midst of the waters;
situated below, the gods and the immortals constantly regard one another with contempt.
That which is sunrise in Laṅkā is sunset in Siddhapura;
it is midday at Yamakoṭi, and it would be midnight in the region of Romaka.
Lanka lies at one-fourth of the terrestrial zone from the center of land and sea;
Ujjayinī is situated at one-fourth of the distance from Lanka, directly to the north.
The visible half of the celestial sphere (bhagolārdha) is deficient by half the diameter of the earth when measured from a level location;
the other half is hidden by the earth and exceeds that same measure by half the diameter of the earth.
The gods, situated on the northern Meru, see the half of the stellar sphere (bhagola) moving clockwise;
however, the pretas in the southern Mare’s Mouth see the other half moving counter-clockwise.
The gods see the risen sun for half a solar year; likewise, the *pretas* [see it] for half a lunar month;
the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) for half a lunar month; and here on earth, human beings [see it] for half a civil day (*kudinam*).
Where the sun rises and sets, there are circles extending east-west, north-south, downward, and upward,
situated with equal sides on the surface of the earth.

That circle which touches the eastern and western directions and also touches the tips of the two axes arising from the earth is the *unmaṇḍala*, wherein the decrease and increase of day and night occur.
The lines extending east-west, north-south, downward, and upward—
wherever the observer may be situated, he should observe the intersection of these lines.
Above and below the observer, the circle of the visible [heavenly bodies] facing the planet is the circle of the projection of vision;
this circle of the projection of vision would also be the eastern ascendant diminished by three signs.
One should cause a wooden sphere— perfectly round, equal in weight on all sides,
and light— to revolve with mercury, oil, and water, according to one's own intelligence and for a period of time.

One should distinguish the half of the celestial sphere (bhagolārdha) within the hemisphere of the visible sphere (dṛśgola) by means of a semicircle of the [diurnal] arc. The equinoctial sine (viṣuvajīvā) is its base (bhuja), while the declination (akṣa) is its perpendicular (koṭi).
Subtracting the square of the desired declination from the square of half the diameter,
the square root of the remainder is the semi-diameter of the day-and-night circle (ahorātrārdhaviṣkambha) to the north or south of the equator.
The product of the desired jyā and half the equatorial radius (vyāsa) is the final value at the limit of the arc;
this result, divided by half of its own day-and-night period, yields the latitudinal jyā for the eastern sunrise at Laṅkā from the point of origin.
The sine of the ascendant (akṣajyā), multiplied by the desired oblique ascension and divided by the radius (lambaka),
is the sine of the increase or decrease of day and night (kṣayavṛddhijyā) within its own solar day.
For the first and last quarters of the day rise with a quarter of the day lacking its moving foot;
the other two [quarters] rise with that [foot] added, respectively in forward and reverse order.
Having multiplied the sine of the desired [latitude] for one's own day-and-night by the earth-sine (kṣitijā) and divided by the radius (viṣkambha-ardha),
the results are the two shadow-sticks (śaṅku) for the elapsed and remaining portions of the day.
The gnomon at one's desired time, multiplied by the equinoctial sine and divided by its own lambaka,
gives the tip of the solar gnomon to the south of the east-west line (astamaya-udaya-sūtra).
Then, one should divide the maximum declination-cosine, multiplied by the desired sine-half, by the *lambaka*;
the quotient is the sine of the sun’s amplitude, east and west of the terrestrial equator.
If that [equinoctial shadow] is less than the equinoctial sine, it is multiplied by the northern equinoctial gnomon-shadow and divided by the equinoctial sine;
the result is the east-west gnomon-shadows.
The sine of the elevated degrees from the zenith is the other gnomon;
the sine of the depressed degrees from the meridian is the shadow of that very same gnomon.
The product of the mid-sine and the sine of the [longitude] rising, divided by half the diameter,
is such that its square root from the difference of the squares of the mid-sine is the correction for the [longitude of the] zenith (sva-dṛk-kṣepa).

The square root of the difference between the squares of the [correction for the] zenith and the correction for the [longitude of the] zenith is the motion of the zenith (sva-dṛg-gati) due to the influence of the Earth.
On the terrestrial sphere, the shadow of the observer's own location is at a distance from the center of the sky equal to half the terrestrial circumference.
The product of the latitude and the sine of the nonagesimal, divided by the cosine of the altitude, shall be negative when the moon is situated in the northern hemisphere;
at rising it is positive, and at setting, when the moon is in the southern hemisphere, it is positive and then negative.
The ascensional difference, multiplied by the oblique ascensions and divided by half the arc of the amplitude, is positive in the northern solstice and negative in the southern;
it is positive in the northern course and negative in the southern.
The moon is water, the sun is fire, and even the shadow of the earth is darkness;
for the moon obscures the sun, and the great shadow of the earth obscures the moon.
When the moon, approaching its node (pāta), enters the sun at the end of a clear lunar month, then at the end of the fortnight it enters the shadow of the earth;
that is the middle of the eclipse, whether exceeding or falling short [of the calculated time].
One should divide the distance between the Earth and the Sun by the difference between the Sun and the Earth multiplied by the Earth;
the result obtained is the length of the Earth's shadow, measured from the diameter of the terrestrial globe.
One should know that the product of the shadow-tip, the moon’s aperture, and the diameter of the earth,
divided by the shadow of the earth, is the diameter of darkness itself.
The square of the moon’s latitude should be subtracted from half the duration [of the eclipse] caused by contact with the moon;
the square root of this result should be known as the duration [of the partial phase] derived from the daily motion of the moon and sun.
The square of the half of the dark portion [of the moon], diminished by the square of the Moon’s latitude,
when subtracted from that [square], has a square root which is the half of the eclipse duration (vimarda).
Having subtracted from half the diameter of Tamas the half-diameter of the Moon,
that which remains from the displacement is not perceived of the Moon.
The square root of [the quantity] consisting of the middle of the duration increased by the square of the displacement and decreased by the square of the desired [time],
when subtracted from half the total duration, is the instantaneous morsel.
The latitude multiplied by the meridian altitude and divided by half the amplitude is the direction [of the shadow] to the south;
and at the time of contact, it is derived from half the duration of the eclipse, starting from the sun or moon as increased by three signs and the precession.
At the end of the eclipse, the moon becomes smoky-grey; during a partial eclipse, it becomes black;
during a total eclipse, it is tawny; and in the midst of the darkness, it is dark-brown and coppery.
In the conjunction of the solar and lunar halos, the eighth part of the sun [is invisible] and cannot be predicted;
this is because of the sun's brilliant nature and the extreme transparency and thinness of the lunar halo.

One should calculate the sun from the conjunction with the earth (ascendant), and the moon from the conjunction with the sun and moon; likewise, all the lunar mansions and planets [are calculated] from the conjunction of the moon, the lunar mansions, and the planets.

By the grace of Brahmā, I have extracted from the ocean of knowledge concerning the existent and the non-existent this supreme jewel of true knowledge, having dived into it with the boat of my own intellect.
This work, named Āryabhaṭīya, is eternally and perpetually equal to that which was composed by Svayambhū;
for anyone who produces a mere counterfeit of it brings about the destruction of their own well-performed merit and lifespan.
